h1: Beer styles for Indo-Chinese food like chilli chicken and noodles
title: Beer With Indo-Chinese Food | Craft Beer School
desc: Beer styles for chilli chicken, gobi manchurian, hakka noodles and schezwan fried rice, with simple rules for soy, vinegar, garlic and chilli heat.
teaser: Chilli chicken, manchurian and schezwan rice want different beers. Here is which one to order next time.
standfirst: Indo-Chinese food is a cuisine of its own: soy, vinegar, garlic, ginger and green chilli, often fried and glazed. It is also one of the easiest foods to pair with beer once you know what each dish is doing.
sections: What Indo-Chinese food brings to the glass

Indo-Chinese cooking grew out of Kolkata's Chinese community and spread across the country. Its flavour base is consistent: soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, ginger, green chilli and spring onion, often with cornflour batter and a glossy sauce. Many dishes are a little sweet. Some, like anything labelled schezwan, carry serious dried chilli heat.

That gives four things to pair against: salt, sweet and sour sauce, fried batter and chilli. Carbonation handles fried batter. Malt sweetness balances salt and vinegar. Low bitterness keeps chilli in check. Our guide to beer with street food uses the same thinking for chaat and rolls.

Dry chilli chicken is battered chicken tossed with green chilli, onion, capsicum, soy and vinegar. It is salty, garlicky and fairly hot. A crisp pilsner or a rice lager is the safe choice: dry, light and fizzy enough to reset your palate after each piece.

For something more interesting, try a Vienna lager. Its toasty malt softens the soy and vinegar without adding bitterness. Chilli paneer works the same way, though the paneer's milkiness lets you go slightly fuller, towards a helles or a kölsch.
Starters: crispy corn, spring rolls and momos

Most Indo-Chinese meals open with fried starters. Crispy corn comes tossed with salt, pepper and green chilli. Veg spring rolls are all crunch too. Both are mostly oil and texture. They need fizz more than flavour, so a pilsner, rice lager or kölsch is ideal.

Momos come from the Himalayan regions rather than the Indo-Chinese kitchen, but they share the menu almost everywhere. Steamed momos are mild and juicy. The red chutney served with them is often fiercely hot. A hefeweizen or witbier works with the dumpling itself. If you go heavy on the chutney, drink something with low bitterness and keep water nearby.

Honey chilli potato, sweet, sticky and hot, sits closer to a dessert than a starter. An amber ale or a Vienna lager handles the sugar without making the chilli flare.
Gobi manchurian and other gravy dishes

Manchurian, whether gobi, veg balls or chicken, comes dry or in a thick, dark, slightly sweet gravy heavy with garlic and soy. The sweetness and depth call for malt. An amber ale, Märzen or English bitter has the caramel to match.

Sweet and sour dishes, with their bright vinegar and sugar, suit a witbier. Its orange peel and soft body meet the fruity sauce. A gentle fruit beer can work if it is not too sweet.

Hakka noodles and plain fried rice are mild, oily and savoury. Almost any clean lager works. A hefeweizen is a nice option here: its banana and clove notes add something the dish lacks while its fizz lifts the oil.

Schezwan fried rice or schezwan noodles are a different story. The red chilli sauce is hot and garlicky. Choose a beer with low bitterness and some sweetness, like a helles, a Vienna lager or even a milk stout if you want to calm the heat. Hot and sour soup, with its vinegar and white pepper, pairs well with a wheat beer.

People often order an IPA with Indo-Chinese food because the menu suggests bold beer for bold food. With chilli, it usually backfires. Hop bitterness and alcohol both make capsaicin feel hotter, so a 65 IBU IPA can turn a moderate chilli chicken into a punishing one. Our guide to beer and spicy food explains why.

A gentle session IPA or a pale ale at modest bitterness can work with milder dishes like veg hakka noodles, where the citrus hop aroma meets ginger and spring onion. Save the big IPAs for after the chilli.

If a taproom offers a flight, order four small pours and taste them against one or two dishes. You will learn more in twenty minutes than any chart can teach. Notice which beer makes the chilli flare and which one makes the soy taste rounder.

Keep pours small, order plenty of food and some water for the table. Most people can tell when a pairing works but struggle to say why. Putting words to that is what trained tasters learn to do.
faqs: What is the best beer with chilli chicken?
A crisp pilsner or rice lager. For more flavour, try a Vienna lager, whose toasty malt softens soy and vinegar.
Why does IPA make Indo-Chinese food taste hotter?
Hop bitterness and alcohol both increase how hot chilli feels. Low bitterness, slightly sweet beers calm the heat instead.
Which beer goes with gobi manchurian?
A malty beer such as an amber ale, Märzen or English bitter. The caramel in the beer matches the sweet, dark gravy.
